proof.claim:
A publish must produce an artifact the whole cluster can resolve, serve, and
converge on — and must not report a success it has not achieved.

WHY THIS EXISTS. The suite already asserts on the STATE of the repository
after a publish, but never executed one: the bundle arrives pre-published, so
every upgrade scenario until now observed the aftermath of a pipeline it did
not drive. desired-state-refuses-what-it-cannot-resolve covers the operator
half (`services desired set`) and names this scenario for the other half. The
path that failed roughly one run in two on 2026-08-16 is the publish itself,
and it had zero coverage of its execution.

THE TWO FAILURE SHAPES, both from that incident:

1. PUBLISHED but not servable. The manifest authority is cluster-wide, the
   blob store is per-node. A publish materializes bytes only in the CAS of
   the instance that received them; every other node reads the same manifest,
   reports PUBLISHED, and cannot serve it. Whether a deploy worked depended on
   which repository instance served the install — not something the operator
   controls or can see.

2. PUBLISHED twice, resolvable never. Re-publishing an unchanged version
   minted a second build_id for it. The resolver requires exactly one, so the
   version went ambiguous and the rollout stalled — reported as converging,
   forever.

WHY RE-PUBLISHING A STAGED ARCHIVE IS THE RIGHT DRIVER. This is not a
shortcut around building a new binary; it is the exact operation that broke.
The platform's own local-deploy model is "reuse an existing published release
version and advance only the build identity", so a second publish of one
version is the normal case, not an abuse of it. Building a genuinely new
binary would require a Go toolchain in the node image and would test the
compiler rather than the pipeline. The archive is taken from
/var/lib/globular/packages/ — the staged CAS is the only sanctioned package
source (repository.minio_is_not_valid_package_source).

WHY dns. `desired set` is known to refuse `blog` with a kind error its own
resolver contradicts (desired_state.refusal_message_misattributes_cause).
desired-state-refuses-what-it-cannot-resolve settled on dns as a target the
platform genuinely accepts; reusing it here keeps this scenario failing on
the property under test rather than on a known diagnostic bug.

WHY candidate, AND WHY NOT A local@ PUBLISHER. Identity lanes are enforced in
local_publish_guard.go: stable is publisher=core@globular.io + channel=STABLE
+ clean semver and is SEALED; dev is publisher=local@<id> + channel=DEV + a
+local./-dev. version suffix; hotfix is any publisher + CANDIDATE + a -hotfix.
suffix. This scenario publishes to CANDIDATE under the archive's own
publisher, which is what `globular deploy` itself does by default
("candidate; stable forbidden") — it is the real deploy lane, and it trips
none of the four identity rules.

It deliberately does NOT publish as local@<cluster-id>. That lane is correct
for a developer testing an unreleased binary, but it MINTS A PUBLISHER
NAMESPACE as a side effect of publishing, and a publisher namespace is an
RBAC-owned resource, not a free string
(package.publisher_namespace_is_rbac_resource). A scenario that ran on every
suite execution would accumulate unclaimed namespaces in the repository it is
supposed to be validating. Re-publishing identical bytes under the existing
publisher creates no new identity at all, which is the property that makes
this safe to run repeatedly.

WHAT THIS PINS. After a publish: the blob is reachable from every node, the
version still resolves to exactly one artifact, desired state can be pointed
at it, and every node reports that version installed. The publish reports
SUCCESS only when it achieved one — exit code alone is not accepted as proof.

NOT COVERED HERE, and worth stating plainly: the desired-state REGRESSION
floor, which needs two published versions of one package. A bundle ships one
version per package, so a second version cannot be produced without building
one — see the note in desired-state-refuses-what-it-cannot-resolve. This
scenario advances build identity, not release version, and asserts nothing
about rollback.

authority.note: Simulation output is evidence/candidate knowledge only. Governed promotion is required before production may rely on it.
